en.title: Chris Hansen Crashes 'Primetime' Screening, Calls Fictionalized Portrayal 'An Insult'
en.summary: The former 'To Catch a Predator' host secretly attended a screening of the new A24 film 'Primetime' and didn't hold back his criticism. Hansen claims the movie's depiction of his work is a complete fabrication.
en.body:
In a move that sounds ripped straight from one of his own investigations, **Chris Hansen** made a surprise appearance at a packed Times Square theater to secretly watch **'Primetime'**, the A24 film dramatizing his career. While many in the audience were unaware of the former **'To Catch a Predator'** host's presence, Hansen himself was taking notes, ready to share his unfiltered thoughts.

His immediate reaction, teased on X (formerly Twitter), was anything but complimentary. "Well….I saw Primetime," Hansen posted, announcing his intention to discuss his critique on his podcast, **'Have A Seat With Chris Hansen'**. This clandestine viewing comes after Hansen reportedly refused to sign an NDA for the film, indicating a deep-seated objection to its portrayal. He has been vocal about his disapproval, stating that key phrases and moments depicted in the film, including the iconic "Have a seat," are entirely fictionalized and do not reflect actual events from his investigative work. The film, which began airing on NBC on September 25, 2026, aims to capture the essence of Hansen's groundbreaking series, but from Hansen's perspective, it misses the mark entirely.

## A Fictionalized Legacy?

**Chris Hansen**'s objection to **'Primetime'** centers on what he perceives as a gross misrepresentation of his investigative methods and personal experiences. Having not officially seen the film prior to its public release, his decision to attend a screening incognito speaks volumes about his concern for how his work is being presented to a new generation of viewers. The film's premise, which uses his story as a jumping-off point, has clearly rubbed him the wrong way. He has explicitly stated that the depiction is "a complete work of fiction," suggesting that the narrative strays significantly from the reality of his efforts to expose predators. This fictionalization, he believes, is not just inaccurate but an "insult" to the victims and the integrity of the investigations themselves.

## Fan Reaction and the Stakes of True Storytelling

For fans of **Chris Hansen** and the true-crime genre, **'Primetime'** presents a fascinating, albeit contentious, case study. The debate now shifts to how much creative license filmmakers can take when adapting real-life figures and events, especially when those individuals are still alive and actively speaking out. The core question for viewers is whether the film's narrative enhancements serve the story or undermine the credibility of the subject matter. Hansen's strong reaction is likely to fuel discussions within the online community, with many eager to compare the film's portrayal with their understanding of his past work. The stakes are high for both the filmmakers, who risk alienating their subject and a segment of the audience, and for Hansen, whose public image and the legacy of his impactful series are on the line.

## What's Next

**Chris Hansen** is expected to delve deeper into his criticisms on his podcast and YouTube channel. Further details regarding **'Primetime'** and any potential responses from the filmmakers are anticipated as the film continues its release and garners more audience attention.
